question: Which Portuguese navigator, in 1498, became the first European to reach India by sailing around the southern tip of Africa?
topic: Famous explorers and voyages of discovery
source_excerpt: Da Gama finally accomplished the feat when he landed at Kozhikode on 20 May 1498.

extra.why_interesting: Players know Columbus sailed west looking for India; the man who actually got there by sea, going the other way round Africa, is the one who changed world trade.
extra.verification_notes: Vasco da Gama reached Calicut on 20 May 1498 as the first European to arrive by the sea route around Africa; the question's wording excludes the earlier overland travellers.

explanation: Da Gama landed at Calicut on India's southwest coast, giving Portugal the sea route to Asian spices that Columbus had failed to find by going west.

question: On which Pacific islands was the British navigator James Cook killed in 1779, during his third great voyage?
topic: Famous explorers and voyages of discovery
source_excerpt: Cook and four marines were killed in the affray and left on the shore.

extra.why_interesting: The man who charted New Zealand and Australia's east coast did not die at sea or at home, but in a beach skirmish on a holiday island everyone can name.
extra.verification_notes: Cook was killed 14 Feb 1779 at Kealakekua Bay, Hawaiʻi Island, in the Hawaiian Islands, on his third voyage (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Cook).

explanation: Cook died in a fight with islanders at Kealakekua Bay on the Big Island of Hawaii, after a dispute over a stolen boat turned violent.

question: What was the name of Ernest Shackleton's ship, crushed by Antarctic pack ice and sunk in 1915?
topic: Famous explorers and voyages of discovery
source_excerpt: sank following crush by pack ice on 21 November 1915.

extra.why_interesting: The ship's name is a famous piece of irony: the vessel named for toughness was destroyed by ice, yet the crew lived up to the name instead.
extra.verification_notes: Endurance was crushed by Weddell Sea pack ice and sank 21 November 1915; the wreck was found in 2022, which doesn't affect the answer (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endurance_(1912_ship)).

explanation: The Endurance went down in the Weddell Sea, yet every one of the 28 men survived, after Shackleton sailed a small open boat some 1,300 kilometres to fetch help.

question: In May 1953, New Zealander Edmund Hillary and Sherpa Tenzing Norgay became the first people confirmed to stand on the top of which mountain?
topic: Famous explorers and voyages of discovery
source_excerpt: On 29 May 1953, he and Edmund Hillary were the first people confirmed to have reached the summit of Mount Everest

extra.why_interesting: A great twentieth-century exploration first that most adults have heard of; the delight is remembering it was a two-man partnership, not a solo hero.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Hillary and Tenzing were the first confirmed to summit Mount Everest on 29 May 1953; the question's 'confirmed' wording handles the Mallory and Irvine 1924 uncertainty.

explanation: Hillary and Tenzing reached the 8,849-metre summit on the 29th of May 1953, and the news reached London just in time for Queen Elizabeth's coronation.

question: Marco Polo's famous book about his travels to the court of Kublai Khan was dictated to a fellow inmate while Polo was being held where?
topic: Famous explorers and voyages of discovery
source_excerpt: He spent several months of his imprisonment dictating a detailed account of his travels to a fellow inmate, Rustichello da Pisa.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture the famous travel book written at a Venetian desk; in fact it was told from a prison cell to a cellmate, after Polo was captured in a sea battle.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Polo dictated the account to fellow inmate Rustichello da Pisa while imprisoned by the Genoese; the answer 'in prison' is generic but correct.

explanation: Polo was captured by Genoa after a sea battle with Venice, and in a Genoese prison he told his stories to the romance writer Rustichello da Pisa, who wrote them down.

question: When Bartolomeu Dias first rounded the southern tip of Africa in 1488, he gave it a gloomier name than the one it carries today. What did he call it?
topic: Famous explorers and voyages of discovery
source_excerpt: Tradition has it that Dias originally named it the Cape of Storms (Cabo das Tormentas) and that King John II later renamed it the Cape of Good Hope

extra.why_interesting: The cheerful name on every map today was a royal rebranding; the man who actually sailed round it chose something far more honest.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's Bartolomeu Dias article says he originally named it Cape of Storms (Cabo das Tormentas) and John II renamed it Cape of Good Hope; the 'tradition' hedge and the loose 'southern tip' wording are minor.

explanation: Dias named it after the foul weather that nearly wrecked him, but King John II of Portugal renamed it the Cape of Good Hope to advertise the promise of a sea route to India.

question: Years before he reached the South Pole, Roald Amundsen became the first person to sail all the way through which long-sought Arctic sea route north of Canada?
topic: Famous explorers and voyages of discovery
source_excerpt: In 1903, Amundsen led the first expedition to traverse Canada's Northwest Passage between the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone files Amundsen under the South Pole; few realise he had already solved the centuries-old Arctic puzzle that had killed Franklin's expedition.
extra.verification_notes: Amundsen's Gjøa expedition (1903–1906) was the first to traverse the Northwest Passage, years before reaching the South Pole in 1911.

explanation: Amundsen took the tiny ship Gjøa through the passage between 1903 and 1906, succeeding where John Franklin's expedition had vanished sixty years earlier.

question: Three of these navigators personally sailed all the way around the world. Which one never did?
topic: Famous explorers and voyages of discovery
source_excerpt: Magellan died on April 27, 1521, in the Philippines during the Battle of Mactan

extra.why_interesting: The name most associated with the first voyage around the world belongs to the one man on the list who never finished one.
extra.verification_notes: Magellan died at Mactan in 1521; Elcano, Drake and Cavendish each completed a circumnavigation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Magellan).

explanation: Magellan was killed on the island of Mactan in the Philippines in 1521, halfway round. Elcano brought his expedition home, and Drake and Cavendish later completed their own circumnavigations.

question: The only confirmed Viking settlement in North America, dating from around the year 1000, was excavated at L'Anse aux Meadows. In which modern country is it?
topic: Famous explorers and voyages of discovery
source_excerpt: L'Anse aux Meadows is the only confirmed Norse site in North America outside Greenland.

extra.why_interesting: Players know the Vikings 'got to America first' but rarely know the one place where archaeology actually proves it, and that it is Canadian, not American.
extra.verification_notes: L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, Canada, is still the only confirmed Norse site in North America outside Greenland, and no newer confirmed site has been found (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%27Anse_aux_Meadows).

explanation: The site sits at the northern tip of Newfoundland and is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site, the physical proof that Norse sailors reached the Americas five centuries before Columbus.

question: Which English explorer was cast adrift in a small boat by his mutinous crew in 1611, in the great Canadian bay that now carries his name?
topic: Famous explorers and voyages of discovery
source_excerpt: set Hudson, his teenage son John, and seven crewmen—men who were either sick and infirm or loyal to Hudson—adrift from Discovery in a small shallop

extra.why_interesting: A huge sea on the world map carries the name of a man whose own crew abandoned him there to die; the geography is the clue to the name.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Hudson was set adrift in a shallop by mutineers in 1611 in Hudson Bay, which is named after him.

explanation: Hudson, his teenage son and seven others were set adrift and never seen again, while the mutineers sailed the ship home to England.

question: Roughly 270 men sailed from Spain with Magellan's fleet in 1519. About how many of them came home on the single ship that completed the voyage around the world in 1522?
topic: Famous explorers and voyages of discovery
source_excerpt: 18 men returned to Seville aboard Victoria in 1522

extra.why_interesting: Players expect heavy losses on a three-year voyage, but the sheer scale, with fewer than one in ten coming home, is still a shock.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia reports about 270 men departing and only 18 returning aboard Victoria (about 21 with three Moluccans), both under 25.

explanation: Just 18 survivors reached Spain aboard the Victoria under Juan Sebastián Elcano, after scurvy, battles, desertions and a shipwreck had claimed the rest and four of the five ships.

question: Decades before Portuguese ships reached the Indian Ocean, which Chinese admiral led seven huge fleet voyages that sailed as far as the east coast of Africa?
topic: Famous explorers and voyages of discovery
source_excerpt: commanded seven treasure voyages across Asia

extra.why_interesting: Players assume long-range exploration began with Portugal and Spain; a Chinese fleet was visiting East Africa decades before Dias rounded the Cape.
extra.verification_notes: Zheng He commanded seven treasure voyages (1405–1433) reaching East Africa, decades before da Gama's 1498 arrival, per Wikipedia.

explanation: Between 1405 and 1433 Zheng He's treasure fleets visited India, Arabia and East African ports such as Malindi, and one voyage famously brought a giraffe back to the Ming emperor.

question: Which 14th-century scholar from Tangier spent nearly thirty years travelling around 120,000 kilometres across Africa, the Middle East, India and China, out-distancing Marco Polo?
topic: Famous explorers and voyages of discovery
source_excerpt: totalling around 117,000 km (73,000 mi), surpassing Zheng He with about 50,000 km (31,000 mi) and Marco Polo with 24,000 km (15,000 mi).

extra.why_interesting: Marco Polo gets the fame, but a Moroccan contemporary out-travelled him by a wide margin, and his name is a genuine reach for a well-read player.
extra.verification_notes: Ibn Battuta, a scholar from Tangier, travelled about 30 years and roughly 117,000 km (about 120,000 km), well beyond Marco Polo's 24,000 km.

explanation: Ibn Battuta set out for Mecca in 1325 and kept going for almost three decades, and his dictated account, the Rihla, remains a key record of the medieval Islamic world.

question: Magellan set out from Spain in 1519 with a fleet of five ships. How many of those ships made it all the way around the world and back to Spain in 1522?
topic: Famous explorers and voyages of discovery

extra.why_interesting: Players picture the 'first voyage around the world' as a triumphant fleet coming home; in fact the expedition was nearly wiped out, with a single battered ship and a skeleton crew limping back, and Magellan himself not among them.

explanation: Only the Victoria returned, carrying just 18 of the roughly 270 men who had set out, and Magellan himself had been killed in the Philippines a year earlier.

question: Antonio Pigafetta kept a careful day-by-day diary on Magellan's expedition. When the last surviving ship reached Spain in 1522 after sailing west around the globe, by how much was his diary out of step with the calendar at home?
topic: Famous explorers and voyages of discovery
source_excerpt: We were greatly surprised for it was Wednesday with us, and we could not see how we had made a mistake

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a meticulous diary cannot drift from the calendar. The answer makes them realise that sailing around the world westward quietly costs you a full day, a problem nobody had met before because nobody had done it before, and the international date line did not yet exist to fix it.
extra.verification_notes: Pigafetta's diary said Wednesday when the Portuguese at Cape Verde said Thursday (9 July 1522), a one-day lag from circumnavigating westward; source https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_First_Voyage_Round_the_World/Pigafetta's_Account_of_Magellan's_Voyage

explanation: Sailing steadily westward, the crew had lost a full day without noticing, and no international date line yet existed to account for it. Pigafetta thought he had made a counting error until the explanation was worked out.
